topic.title: Quadratic graphs: plotting, reading and intersections with straight lines
topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M7 and M8 are each two 75-minute papers of 50 marks. One quadratic-graph question appears in most series, worth 6 to 10 marks in four or five parts, and it runs the same route every time: complete the table (1 to 2 marks), draw the curve (2), solve from the graph (1), draw a line (1), read the intersections (2), and on M8 a closing part asking which line solves a related equation (2). Plotting and the smooth curve carry separate marks; readings are marked from the candidate's own curve; the closing part is marked MA1 for the rearrangement and A1 for the line, and the reports place it among the last parts attempted.
mustMemorise: Square a negative x first, then the x term, then the constant
Plot every point, then one smooth freehand curve, dipping below the two lowest points
Solving means y = 0: read both crossings of the x-axis
A line needs its own table of two or three points, drawn with a ruler right across the grid
Intersections are points: give both coordinates for both of them
For a new equation, rearrange until one side is the drawn curve; the other side is the line
onFormulaSheet: The quadratic formula (page 2), which is not the method for this statement
notOnThisSpec: Solving the quadratic algebraically when the question says to use the graph: the marks are for the reading, and the formula belongs to M4-NA-05
Curves other than quadratics meeting lines: M7-NA-10 names quadratic functions and lines of the form y = mx + c
Finding the turning point by completing the square or by differentiation: at M7 it comes from symmetry or from the graph
Intersections found by solving the simultaneous equations algebraically, which is M8-NA-09

mustBeAbleTo: Complete a table of values for a quadratic, including negative values of x
Plot the points and join them with one smooth curve that dips below the two lowest plotted points
Use the graph to solve a quadratic equation by reading both crossings of the x-axis
Read a y value at a given x, and the minimum or maximum value, to the accuracy the grid allows
Draw a line y = mx + c on the same grid from a small table of values, extended right across
Write down the coordinates of both points where a line meets a curve
Rearrange a different quadratic equation to decide which straight line to draw, then read its solutions
sheet.howExamined: One long question on Paper 1 or Paper 2, usually 6 to 10 marks in four or five parts, and it follows the same route every series: complete the table, draw the curve, solve from the graph, draw a line, read the intersections, and on M8 a final part asking which line solves a related equation (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q10 and M8 Paper 1 Q4; November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q15 and M8 Paper 1). Plotting and the smooth curve carry separate marks, readings are marked from the candidate's own curve, and the rearrangement part is marked MA1 for the method and A1 for the line.
traps: Table values that slip for negative x, from the squared term or from the x term (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1, November 2025 M8 Paper 1)
Points joined with a ruler, or a flat bottom between the two lowest points (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1, November 2025 M7 Paper 2)
Only one root given where both were needed (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 and M8 Paper 1)
The required line not drawn, or a horizontal line drawn instead (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1)
Substituting into the equation when the question said to use the graph (November 2025 M7 Paper 2)
A minimum written as 0 when the curve clearly dips below the axis, or the scale misread (November 2025 M7 Paper 2 and M8 Paper 1)
Drawing the line across the curve and then not writing down where the two meet: both crossings are wanted, as coordinate pairs, and very few candidates got that far (Summer 2024 M7 Paper 1 Q10)

Not working out which line to draw when a different equation has to be solved from the same curve: rearrange that equation until one side is the curve's equation, and whatever is left on the other side is the line (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q4)
Reading a value off the grid as though every small square were 0.1 when the scale is 0.2; count the squares between two printed labels before you take any reading (November 2025 M7 Paper 2 Q15)

Losing the minimum to the scale: only about 35% of candidates read it correctly, so work out what one small square is worth on the y-axis before you read the lowest point of your curve (November 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q7)

workedExamples.stem: Complete the table of values for $y=x^{2}+x-5$ for $x$ from $-3$ to $3$, then plot the curve.

steps.decision: Do a negative substitution in three separate pieces rather than in one line. The square is positive, the $x$ term keeps its minus sign, and the constant is unchanged. This is the single most reported slip in the table.

options: Because $(-3)^{2}$ is positive while $+x$ stays negative
Because squaring always makes a number smaller
Because the minus sign cancels the constant
whyMenu.explain: Squaring a negative gives a positive, -3 squared is 9, but the $+x$ term is still $-3$. Mixing those two up is what produces the wrong table values the examiners report.

steps.decision: The easy cell is worth doing next because it anchors the middle of the curve: the constant term is always the value at $x=0$.
Look along the finished row before plotting. The values fall and then rise, and two of them are equal, which tells you where the lowest point of the curve is going to be.

steps.working: Lowest point halfway between $x=-1$ and $x=0$: $x=-0.5$ gives $y=-5.25$
steps.decision: Work out that one extra value before drawing. The two equal entries are at $y=-5$, and the curve has to dip to $-5.25$ between them, so the bottom is rounded, not flat, and it is drawn freehand.

options: Because the turning point lies between the two equal values, not at either of them
Because tables always miss a point
Because the curve is steeper on the left
whyMenu.explain: A parabola is symmetrical, so with equal values at $x=-1$ and $x=0$ the turning point is at $x=-0.5$. Examiners report flat bottoms and ruled joins between these two points every series.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The table reads 1, -3, -5, -5, -3, 1, 7, and the curve dips to $(-0.5, -5.25)$ between the two equal values

twin.stem: Complete the table for $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ at $x=-2$ and $x=-1$, giving the two values in order.

workedExamples.stem:
The graph of $y=x^{2}-4x+1$ is drawn.
Use it to estimate the value of $y$ when $x=3.4$, and the minimum value of $y$.

figure.alt: A U-shaped curve on a grid with x from -1 to 5 and y from -4 to 6, each large square is 1 across and 1 up, with five small squares to a large one, so each small square is 0.2 across and 0.2 up. The curve passes through (-1, 6), (0, 1), (1, -2), (2, -3), (3, -2), (4, 1), (5, 6) and dips to its lowest point at (2, -3), between the plotted points at x = 1 and x = 3.

steps.working: Scale: one large square across is 1, one large square up is 1, so one small square up is $0.2$
steps.decision: Read the scale before reading anything else. The reports keep naming the scale as the thing that goes wrong, and it takes five seconds to settle: count the small squares between two printed numbers.

steps.working: Up from $x=3.4$ (two small squares past 3) to the curve, then across: $y \approx -1.0$
steps.decision: Draw the two lines on the graph rather than doing it by eye. They are free to draw, they show the examiner where the reading came from, and they stop you drifting to the nearest plotted point.

options: Because the question said to use the graph, and the lines are the evidence
Because the lines earn a mark of their own
Because the curve is hard to see
whyMenu.explain: Substituting into the equation gives $-1.040$, which is the same size, but the November 2025 report says it earned nothing where the question named the graph.

steps.working: Lowest plotted points: $(1, -2)$ and $(3, -2)$, both at $y=-2$
steps.decision: For the minimum, find the two equal values first. The turning point sits halfway between them, which is where to look; it is not at either plotted point.

steps.working: Halfway is $x=2$, and reading down there gives $y \approx -3$
steps.decision: Read the lowest point of the curve, not the lowest point you plotted, and do not round it up to zero because it is below the axis. The completed square $(x-2)^{2}-3$ confirms $-3$.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: $y \approx -1.0$ at $x=3.4$, and the minimum value of $y$ is about $-3$

workedExamples.stem:
The graph of $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ is drawn on a grid.
Draw the line $y=2x-3$ and write down, as coordinates, the two points where it meets the curve.

figure.alt: A U-shaped curve on a grid with x from -2 to 4 and y from -5 to 6, each large square is 1 across and 1 up, with five small squares to a large one, so each small square is 0.2 across and 0.2 up. The curve passes through the seven points of the table, crosses the x-axis at -1 and 3, and dips to its lowest point at (1, -4).

steps.decision: Make a three-point table for the line instead of guessing its slope. The Summer 2024 report noted candidates who drew a horizontal line here; a table makes that impossible and takes a few seconds.

steps.working: Plot the three points, join with a ruler, extend to both edges of the grid
steps.decision: Extend the line right across the grid. A short line can miss one of the two crossings entirely, and the second crossing carries its own mark.
Read both, and give each as a coordinate pair. A question asking for points of intersection wants both numbers of each pair, not just the $x$ values.

options: Because a line cuts a parabola in two places
Because the line passes through the origin
whyMenu.explain: Unless the line just touches or misses the curve, there are two crossings, and the Summer 2024 report found very few candidates wrote down both.

steps.decision: Check the readings with algebra when the numbers are friendly. The equation the crossings satisfy is the curve set equal to the line, and here it factorises, which confirms both readings exactly.

twin.stem: On the same curve $y=x^{2}-2x-3$, the line $y=1-x$ is drawn. Write down the $x$ value of the right-hand crossing, to 1 decimal place.

figure.alt: The curve y = x² − 2x − 3 on the same grid as the example, x from -2 to 4 and y from -5 to 6, each small square 0.2 across and 0.2 up, with the straight line y = 1 − x drawn as a dashed line from (-2, 3) down to (4, -3). The line crosses the curve twice.

workedExamples.stem:
The graph of $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ is already drawn.
Which straight line would you draw on the same grid to solve $x^{2}-x-6=0$?

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox="0 0 480 164" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g font-family="inherit" font-size="12.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="10" y="22">Rearranging until one side is the curve you already have</text></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="13.5" fill="currentColor"><text x="14" y="52" xml:space="preserve">you want:            x²-x-6 = 0</text><text x="14" y="78" xml:space="preserve">you have drawn:      y = x² - 2x - 3</text><text x="14" y="104" xml:space="preserve">subtract:            (x² - 2x - 3) - (-x + 3) = x^{2}-x-6</text><text x="14" y="130" xml:space="preserve">so draw:             y = -x + 3</text></g><path d="M10 142L470 142" stroke="currentColor" stroke-opacity="0.3" stroke-width="0.9" fill="none"/></svg>
figure.alt: Four lines of working. The first reads: you want x squared minus x minus 6 equals 0. The second reads: you have drawn y equals x squared minus 2x minus 3. The third shows the curve expression minus the line expression giving x squared minus x minus 6. The fourth reads: so draw y equals minus x plus 3.

steps.decision: Write the two down together before doing anything. The curve on the grid cannot change, so the only question is what has to be drawn against it, and that is easier to see with both expressions side by side.
Subtract the equation you want from the curve you have. The $x^{2}$ terms cancel — they must, or no straight line could do the job — and what is left is the line.

options: Because the leftover has no $x^{2}$ term, so it is a straight line
Because subtraction is always the right move
Because the constant must be zero
whyMenu.explain: Both expressions start with $x^{2}$, so subtracting removes it. What remains has only an $x$ term and a number, which is exactly the form $y=mx+c$.

steps.working: So $x^{2}-2x-3 = -x + 3$ at the solutions, and the line is $y=-x + 3$
steps.decision: Say why it works in one sentence: where the curve and this line meet, their $y$ values are equal, so the difference between the two expressions is zero there — and that difference is the equation being solved.

steps.working: Check: the curve and $y=-x + 3$ meet where $x^{2}-2x-3=-x + 3$, that is $x^{2}-x-6=0$, whose solutions are $x=-2$ and $x=3$
steps.decision: Check by solving the target equation independently. Factorising $x^{2}-x-6$ gives $(x+2)(x-3)$, so the crossings should be at $-2$ and $3$ — read those off the drawn graph to confirm.

twin.stem: With the same curve $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ drawn, which line would you draw to solve $x^{2}-2x-5=0$?

items.stem: In the table for $y=x^{2}-2x-3$, what is $y$ when $x=-2$?
items.skill: Substitute a negative x into a quadratic

options.feedback: One of the two signs has gone: either the squared term was made negative, or the $-2x$ term was taken as $-4$. Both give $-3$. Squaring $-2$ gives $4$, and $-2 \times (-2)$ also gives $4$, so the total is $5$.
Both signs have gone: the square was made negative and the $-2x$ term was worked out as $-2 \times 2$. Deal with the sign once, inside the bracket, and every term follows: $5$.

items.stem: Two plotted points of a curve are $(-1, -5)$ and $(0, -5)$, and they are the lowest two. What does the curve do between them?
items.skill: Draw the turning point between two equal values

options.text: Dips below both, to about $-5.25$
options.feedback: Correct. The turning point is halfway between, at $x=-0.5$, where $y=-5.25$.

options.text: Runs flat between them
options.feedback: A parabola has one lowest point, not a level stretch. Substituting $x=-0.5$ gives $-5.25$, below both points.

options.text: Is joined by a ruled line
options.feedback: Ruled joins lose the curve mark. Join plotted points freehand in one smooth sweep.

items.stem: A question says: use the graph to solve $x^{2}-2x-3=0$. Where do you look?
items.skill: Turn an equation into a place on the graph

options.text: Where the curve crosses the $x$-axis
options.feedback: Correct. The equation sets $y$ to zero, and $y=0$ is the $x$-axis.

options.text: At the lowest point of the curve
options.feedback: The lowest point is where the curve stops falling, at $y=-4$ here, not where $y$ is zero.

options.text: Where the curve crosses the $y$-axis
options.feedback: That crossing has $x=0$, which answers a different question. Setting $y=0$ points you at the horizontal axis.

items.stem: A curve crosses the $x$-axis twice and you are asked to solve the equation. How many answers do you write?

options.text: Two
options.feedback: Correct. Both crossings are solutions, and schemes normally need both for the mark.

options.text: One, the positive one
options.feedback: Under half of the Summer 2024 entry gave both. A negative solution counts exactly as much as a positive one.

options.text: One, the one nearer the origin
options.feedback: There is nothing to choose between them: every crossing where $y=0$ solves the equation.

items.stem: A question says: use your graph to estimate $y$ when $x=3.4$. What earns the mark?

options.text: A reading taken from the curve, with lines drawn up and across
options.feedback: Correct. The instruction names the method, and the drawn lines show where the value came from.

options.text: Substituting to get $-1.04$
options.feedback: The November 2025 report says this scored nothing. The value is right, but the question asked for the graph.

options.text: The value at the nearest plotted point
options.feedback: The curve is continuous, so read at the value asked for, not at the nearest point you happened to plot.

items.stem: The $y$-axis is labelled every 1 unit, with five small squares to each label. What is one small square worth?
items.skill: Read the scale before reading a value

options.feedback: Correct. One unit shared into five is $0.2$ per small square.
That would need ten small squares to the unit. Count the squares between two printed numbers before reading anything.
That is the value of a large square here. Reading small squares as units is the error the reports name most often.

items.stem: A curve dips below the $x$-axis. A question asks for the minimum value of $y$. Which answer is being looked for?
items.skill: Read a minimum that is below the axis

options.text: The negative value at the lowest point of the curve
options.feedback: Correct. The minimum is a $y$ value, and it is perfectly normal for it to be negative.

options.text: Zero, because the curve reaches the axis
options.feedback: Many candidates wrote zero in November 2025 even when their own curve clearly dipped below it. The axis is where $y=0$, not where the curve stops.

options.text: The $x$ value of the lowest point
options.feedback: That is where the minimum happens, not the minimum itself. The question asks for the value of $y$.

items.stem: The curve $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ is drawn. Which line solves $x^{2}-2x-5=0$?

options.feedback: Correct. $x^{2}-2x-5=0$ can be written $x^{2}-2x-3=2$, and the left side is the curve already drawn.
The constant from the new equation has been copied straight down. Compare the two expressions: they differ by 2, so the line is $y=2$.
That is a curve, not a line, and you cannot draw a second curve accurately by hand. Subtract until the $x^{2}$ terms cancel.

parts.stem:
A table of values is being filled in for $y=x^{2}-2x-3$.
Work out the value of $y$ when $x=-2$.
hints: Square first: $(-2)^{2}=4$.
Then the $x$ term: $-2 \times (-2) = 4$.
Add the three parts, watching the signs.
parts.workedSolution: Substitute $x=-2$ one term at a time. $(-2)^{2}=4$. The $x$ term gives $-2 \times (-2) = 4$. With the constant $-3$ the total is $4 + 4 - 3 = 5$.

commonErrors.feedback: Either the squared term was made negative or the sign was dropped from the $x$ term; both land on $-3$ here. Squaring a negative gives a positive, $(-2)^{2}=4$, and $-2 \times (-2) = 4$, so the total is $5$.
Both signs have gone: the square was made negative and the $x$ term was worked out from $2$ rather than $-2$. Deal with the sign once, inside the bracket, and the total is $5$.

parts.stem:
A table of values is being filled in for $y=x^{2}-2x-3$.
Work out the value of $y$ when $x=-1$.
hints: Square first: $(-1)^{2}=1$.
Then the $x$ term: $-2 \times (-1) = 2$.
Add the three parts, watching the signs.
parts.workedSolution: Substitute $x=-1$ one term at a time. $(-1)^{2}=1$. The $x$ term gives $-2 \times (-1) = 2$. With the constant $-3$ the total is $1 + 2 - 3 = 0$.

commonErrors.feedback: The square of a negative number is positive: $(-1)^{2}=1$, not $-1$. Squaring first, before any minus signs are dealt with, gives $0$.
The sign of $x$ was kept for the squared term but dropped in the $x$ term. Both need it: $-2 \times (-1) = 2$, which gives $0$.

parts.stem:
A table of values is being filled in for $y=x^{2}+x-5$.
Work out the value of $y$ when $x=-3$.
hints: Square first: $(-3)^{2}=9$.
Then the $x$ term: $1 \times (-3) = -3$.
Add the three parts, watching the signs.
parts.workedSolution: Substitute $x=-3$ one term at a time. $(-3)^{2}=9$. The $x$ term gives $1 \times (-3) = -3$. With the constant $-5$ the total is $9 - 3 - 5 = 1$.

commonErrors.feedback: The square of a negative number is positive: $(-3)^{2}=9$, not $-9$. Squaring first, before any minus signs are dealt with, gives $1$.
The sign of $x$ was kept for the squared term but dropped in the $x$ term. Both need it: $1 \times (-3) = -3$, which gives $1$.

parts.stem:
The graph of $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ is shown.
Use the graph to solve the equation $x^{2}-2x-3=0$.
hints: The equation asks when $y$ is 0.
On the graph, $y=0$ is the $x$-axis.
The curve meets that axis twice, so there are two answers.
parts.workedSolution: The equation sets $y$ to 0, and every point with $y=0$ lies on the $x$-axis. The curve cuts that axis at $x=-1$ and $x=3$, so those are the two solutions. Substituting back confirms them: $(-1)^{2}-2(-1)-3=0$ and $3^{2}-2(3)-3=0$.

commonErrors.feedback: That solution is right and earns one mark. The curve crosses the axis on both sides of its lowest point, so there is a second solution at $x=-1$.
That is the $x$-coordinate of the lowest point, where $y=-4$ rather than 0. Solving means finding where the curve is level with the $x$-axis, which happens on either side of the minimum.

scheme.for: a reading where the curve crosses the $x$-axis on the left, approximately $-2.8$
scheme.examinerNote: CCEA prints a pair of nearby readings as acceptable; a value inside that band scores.

hints: Find where the curve cuts the $x$-axis on the left of the grid.
It is between $-3$ and $-2$.
Each small square across is 0.2.
parts.workedSolution: The left-hand crossing sits between $x=-3$ and $x=-2$, closer to $-3$. Reading to the nearest small square gives about $-2.8$. (The exact value is $\frac{-1-\sqrt{21}}{2}=-2.791$, so the reading is sound.)

commonErrors.feedback: That is a whole square out. Count the small squares from $-3$: each one is 0.2 across, so the crossing is at about $-2.8$.

parts.stem:
Use the graph to estimate the positive solution of the same equation.
Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

scheme.for: a reading where the curve crosses the $x$-axis on the right, approximately $1.8$

hints: The right-hand crossing is between 1 and 2.
Read across to the nearest small square.
The two solutions are not mirror images: the lowest point is not on the $y$-axis.
parts.workedSolution: The right-hand crossing is between $x=1$ and $x=2$, and reads as about $1.8$. (Exactly, $\frac{-1+\sqrt{21}}{2}=1.791$.)

commonErrors.feedback: That is the first solution with its sign changed. The two crossings are only mirror images when the lowest point sits on the $y$-axis; here it is at $x=-0.5$, so read the right-hand crossing off the graph as well.

parts.stem:
The graph of $y=x^{2}+x-5$ is shown.
From the graph, estimate the minimum value of $y$.

scheme.for: a reading of the lowest point of the curve, approximately $-5.25$
reject: $-5$ read from a plotted point rather than the curve

hints: The minimum is the lowest point the curve reaches, not the lowest point you plotted.
It sits between $x=-1$ and $x=0$.
Each small square down the axis is 0.2.
parts.workedSolution: The two lowest plotted points are $(-1, -5)$ and $(0, -5)$, both at $y=-5$. The curve dips between them, and its lowest point is at $x=-0.5$, halfway between. Reading down from there gives about $-5.25$. (Completing the square gives $(x+0.5)^{2}-5.25$, confirming $-5.25$.)

commonErrors.feedback: Zero is where the curve crosses the $x$-axis, not its lowest point. The curve here dips well below that axis, and the minimum is about $-5.25$.
That is the height of the two lowest plotted points. The curve does not run flat between them; it dips a little lower, to about $-5.25$, which is the value the question wants.

findTheMistake.stem: Cara plotted $y=x^{2}+x-5$ correctly and was then asked for the minimum value of $y$. Her working:
studentWorking: the two lowest points are (-1, -5) and (0, -5), so I joined them with a straight line along the bottom
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The table and the plotting are right, so those marks are safe. The third line flattens the bottom of the curve, and that is where the reading goes wrong. A parabola has exactly one lowest point, and with equal values at $x=-1$ and $x=0$ it sits halfway between them, at $x=-0.5$. Substituting gives $y=-5.25$, which is $0.25$ below the two plotted points, so the curve should dip there and the minimum is $-5.25$, not $-5$.
correction: halfway between x = -1 and x = 0 is x = -0.5
draw the curve dipping through (-0.5, -5.25) and read the minimum as about -5.25
findTheMistake.feedback: The table and the plotting were accurate, which is most of the work. The habit to add is a single extra calculation: whenever two table values come out equal, work out the value halfway between them before drawing, because that is where the turning point is. Examiners reported this exact flat bottom in November 2025 on both units.

findTheMistake.stem: A question read: use your graph to estimate $y$ when $x=2.6$. Ruairi had drawn the curve $y=x^{2}-4x+1$ correctly. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The arithmetic is correct from start to finish, and the value $-2.64$ is a good one. The problem is the first line: the question named the method. Marks here are for a reading taken from the drawn curve, so working from the equation earns nothing however accurate it is. The examiners reported exactly this in November 2025.
correction: find x = 2.6 on the horizontal axis (three small squares past 2 on a 0.2 scale)
draw a line up to the curve and across to the y-axis
read the value, about -2.6, and write that down
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing was wrong with the mathematics, which is worth knowing: the same work in a question that did not name the graph would have scored everything. Read the instruction first, do what it names, and use the equation afterwards as your own check that the reading is sensible.

findTheMistake.stem: The curve $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ was drawn on a grid. Sean was asked which straight line to draw to solve $x^{2}-2x-5=0$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The method is right and the third line is nearly right: the two expressions do differ by 2, and subtracting is the correct move. It has been done the wrong way round. The line you draw must satisfy curve $=$ line at the solutions, so take the target away from the curve: $(x^{2}-2x-3)-(x^{2}-2x-5)=2$, giving $y=2$. Drawing $y=-2$ instead would solve $x^{2}-2x-1=0$, whose solutions are about $-0.41$ and $2.41$ rather than the ones asked for.
correction: the left side is the drawn curve, so draw y = 2
findTheMistake.feedback: The structure of the answer was sound, and the method mark stands for seeing that the two expressions differ by a constant. One safeguard makes it reliable: rearrange the equation you are given until the curve's expression appears on one side by itself, and read the line off the other side. Only the strongest candidates managed this part in Summer 2024, so it is worth the extra line of working.

prompts.prompt: How do you work out a table value for a quadratic when $x$ is negative?
prompts.answer: Square first, keeping the sign inside the bracket, then work out the $x$ term with its sign, then add the constant. Three separate pieces, then one addition.

prompts.prompt: Two table values come out equal. What does that tell you, and what should you do before drawing?
prompts.answer: The turning point lies halfway between those two $x$ values. Work out $y$ there, so the curve dips to the right depth instead of running flat.

prompts.prompt: How do you join the plotted points of a quadratic?
prompts.answer: Freehand, in one smooth curve through every point, with no ruled segments and no flat stretch at the bottom.

prompts.prompt: A question says: use the graph to solve $x^{2}+bx+c=0$. Where do you look?
prompts.answer: At the $x$-axis. Setting $y$ to zero means the crossings of the horizontal axis, and both of them are solutions.

prompts.prompt: Why does substituting into the equation score nothing when the question says to use your graph?
prompts.answer: The instruction names the method, so the mark is for the reading. Substitution can be used afterwards as a check, not instead of the reading.

prompts.prompt: How do you draw a straight line such as $y=2x-3$ on a grid that already has a curve on it?
prompts.answer: Make a small table of two or three points, plot them, join with a ruler and extend the line right across the grid so both crossings show.

prompts.prompt: What do the points of intersection of a curve and a line represent?
prompts.answer: The pairs of values that satisfy both equations at once, so their $x$ values are the approximate solutions of the equation formed by setting the two expressions equal.

prompts.prompt: The curve $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ is drawn. How do you decide which line to draw to solve a different quadratic equation?
prompts.answer: Rearrange the new equation until one side is exactly $x^{2}-2x-3$. Whatever is on the other side is the line to draw.

prompts.prompt: How do you read the minimum value of a curve that dips below the $x$-axis?
prompts.answer: Read the $y$ value at the lowest point of the curve, which is negative. It is not zero, and it is not the height of the lowest plotted point.

prompts.prompt: Before reading any value from a graph, what do you check?
prompts.answer: The scale: count the small squares between two printed numbers on each axis and work out what one small square is worth.

findings.asked: Table of values, plot a quadratic, read its roots, draw a line and read the intersections.
findings.wentWrong: Incorrect y-values (-2, -4) from negative x; points joined with straight lines or a flat bottom between two equal minimum points; only one root given; the line y = 2x - 3 not drawn (a horizontal line appeared); intersections rarely both stated.
findings.rule: Smooth curve through every point; both roots; a table of values for the line.

findings.asked: Table, curve, roots, a line, then which line solves a given equation.
findings.wentWrong: Table and line mostly right; under half read both roots; only the strongest knew which line to draw to solve the given equation.
findings.rule: Rearrange the target equation so one side is the curve's function; the other side is the line to draw.

findings.asked: Plot a quadratic, read a value at x = 2.6 from the graph, and its minimum.
findings.wentWrong: Points ruled together; (1, 0) and (2, 0) joined flat instead of dipping; substituting into the equation instead of using the graph scored nothing; the y-scale of 0.2 was misread; many wrote 0 for a minimum that was clearly below zero.
findings.rule: Use the graph when told to, read the scale, and let the curve dip between roots.

findings.asked: Quadratic graph with negative x-values, readings, minimum, and a harder final part.
findings.wentWrong: Negative substitutions went wrong; straight segments between the lowest points; only 35% read the minimum with the scale; the last part was for the top fifth.
findings.rule: Check signs for negative x; the minimum is on the curve, not at a plotted point.
